nationality_or_literary_tradition: English-Indian; the imperial tale, the ballad and the children's book
literary_identity: Poet, short-story writer and novelist; the greatest English writer of the imperial experience and the youngest winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
biography: Born in Bombay on 30 December 1865; he was brought to England at five and boarded with a family in Southsea whose cruelty he later recorded in 'Baa Baa, Black Sheep', then went to the United Services College at Westward Ho. He returned to India in 1882 and worked as a journalist in Lahore and Allahabad, publishing Departmental Ditties (1886) and Plain Tales from the Hills (1888). He lived in London and Vermont from 1889, married Carrie Balestier in 1892, and wrote the Indian and English stories, the Jungle Books, Kim and the Just So Stories. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1907 and died in London on 18 January 1936.
literary_profile: Kipling made the Empire a literary subject: his Indian stories are written from inside the working of the Anglo-Indian administration, with an exactness about native speech, bureaucracy and violence that no other English writer of the period achieved. His verse — Barrack-Room Ballads, The Seven Seas, Recessional — gave the imperial project its songs and, in 'Recessional' and 'The White Man's Burden', its most troubling self-criticism. His children's books are formal masterpieces, and Kim is the finest English novel of India.
stylistic_characteristics: Terse, concrete narrative; technical and dialect vocabulary; the story as a single hard incident; ballads with a driving refrain; the epigram and the gnomic utterance; a narrator who assumes a community of knowledge with the reader.
intellectual_concerns: Empire and the work of administration; the English in India and the native soldier; machinery, engineering and the modern world; courage, endurance and the code of the man at work; childhood and the loss of India; the supernatural and the uncanny.
historical_significance: Kipling is the central writer of the British Empire and one of the most technically accomplished poets and story-writers in English: Kim, the Jungle Books and the Just So Stories are permanent classics, the Barrack-Room Ballads changed English poetry, and his stories of India are the foundation of the literature of the British in Asia. His politics have made him a contested figure, but his formal mastery is beyond question.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: South African; the colonial novel, the allegory and the feminist treatise
literary_identity: Novelist, allegorist and feminist theorist; the first major writer of the British colonial world in southern Africa and the author of the founding feminist novel of the 1880s.
biography: Born Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner on 24 March 1855 at the Wittebergen mission station in the Cape Colony, the daughter of a German missionary and an English mother. She worked as a governess in the Karoo from 1874, wrote The Story of an African Farm there, and went to England in 1881 to study medicine; ill health ended her medical training and she became a writer instead. She was a friend of Havelock Ellis, Eleanor Marx and Edward Carpenter, wrote Woman and Labour (1911), and returned to South Africa in 1899, where she campaigned against the war and against racial injustice. She died in Cape Town on 11 December 1920.
literary_profile: Schreiner wrote the colonial world from inside the colonial subject: The Story of an African Farm is the first novel to make the South African interior its own place rather than a backdrop, and its three children — Waldo, Em and Lyndall — are among the first fully realised colonial characters in English. She is also the great English allegorist of the 1890s and the first theorist of what she called 'labour' as a problem of women's economic dependency.
stylistic_characteristics: Landscape description of the Karoo that is both exact and visionary; allegory and dream-visual inserted into realistic narrative; a plain, passionate prose; the first-person confession; the woman's argument against marriage as an economic institution.
intellectual_concerns: The position of women and the economics of marriage; the colonial childhood and the empty interior; religion, freethought and the loss of faith; the labour question; race and the native population; empire and the South African war.
historical_significance: Schreiner is the founding figure of South African literature in English and one of the most important feminist writers of the century: The Story of an African Farm is the first colonial novel of the interior, Woman and Labour is a central text of the suffrage movement, and her allegories made her a legend of the 1890s.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Australian; the bush story, the ballad and the Australian vernacular
literary_identity: Poet and short-story writer; the founding writer of Australian national literature in English, and the first great voice of the Australian working man.
biography: Born Henry Archibald Hertzberg Lawson at Grenfell, New South Wales, on 17 June 1867, the son of a Norwegian seaman and a suffragist mother who took the family to Sydney in 1883. He published for the Bulletin, the radical Sydney weekly, from 1887, and in 1892 his mother sent him to Bourke, in the western back country, where a year in the drought gave him the material for the bush stories. He married Bertha Bredt in 1896 and travelled to England, where he published Joe Wilson and His Mates (1901). Alcoholism and deafness destroyed his later years, and he died in Sydney on 2 September 1922.
literary_profile: Lawson wrote the Australian outback as a place of terrible beauty and terrible loneliness: his stories are short, laconic, often anecdotal, and told in the voice of the man who has been there — the swagman, the selector, the shearer, the woman keeping house in a bark hut. His verse is the ballads of the Bulletin school, and 'The Drover's Wife' is the founding story of Australian literature.
stylistic_characteristics: Terse, laconic, anecdotal prose; the dialect of the Australian working man written as it sounds; the subordination of plot to a single scene of endurance; sentiment restrained almost to the point of silence; ballad stanzas and refrains.
intellectual_concerns: The isolation of the bush and the rural woman's endurance; mateship and solidarity; poverty and the swagman's life; the Australian landscape of drought and flood; class and the squatter; alcoholism and defeat.
historical_significance: Lawson is the founding writer of modern Australian literature: 'The Drover's Wife' and the Joe Wilson stories created the Australian short story, his ballads became a national folklore, and his portrait of the bush made the landscape itself a national theme.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English-Australian; the colonial novel, the domestic tale and the woman's memoir
literary_identity: Novelist and poet; one of the most popular and perceptive Australian woman writers of the colonial period.
biography: Born Ada Cambridge at St Germans, Norfolk, on 21 November 1844, the daughter of an English merchant; she married the Anglican clergyman George Frederick Cross in 1870 and sailed with him to Victoria, where they served in parishes in the bush for twenty years. She published twenty-three novels, mostly serialised in the Australian press and then reissued in England, and two volumes of poems. She died in Melbourne on 19 July 1926.
literary_profile: Cambridge wrote the colonial novel as a woman's document: her subject is the ordinary life of the parsonage and the small town — courtship, marriage, childbirth, gossip, the visiting bishop, the drought — and she is unusually frank about the economic realities of marriage and the intellectual starvation of the educated colonial wife. Her memoir Thirty Years in Australia is a central record of the woman colonist's experience.
stylistic_characteristics: Domestic realism with a strong narrative voice; the parsonage and the small town; frankness about money and marriage; the comic observation of the religious and the genteel; a plain and pleasant prose.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage and the woman's lot; the colonial parsonage; class and the gentleman in the colony; religion and clerical poverty; emigration and homesickness; education and the woman's mind.
historical_significance: Cambridge was one of the most widely read Australian novelists of the 1890s and is now recovered as a major woman writer of the colonial period: The Three Miss Kings and Thirty Years in Australia are key texts in the history of Australian women's writing.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian; the English lyric, the ballad and the Indian legend
literary_identity: Poet and translator; the first Indian writer to publish a volume of English poetry, and a pioneer of the Indian-English literary tradition.
biography: Born Toru Dutt in Calcutta on 4 March 1856, the youngest daughter of Govin Chunder Dutt, a Bengali civil servant and poet. She was educated at home and at a school in Nice, and in 1873 travelled through England, France and Italy with her family. Both her sister Aru and her brother Abju died young, and Toru herself died of consumption in Calcutta on 30 August 1877, at twenty-one. Her father published her work after her death.
literary_profile: Toru Dutt's English verse is the first substantial body of Indian poetry written in English: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields is a volume of translations from French verse, and Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan retells the Sanskrit epics and Puranic tales in English ballad form. She writes between two traditions — French romanticism, the Sanskrit epic and the Victorian lyric — and her short life made her a founding figure of Indian writing in English.
stylistic_characteristics: Ballad and lyric metres with a French and English formal discipline; narrative verse on the Indian epics; the plain retelling of the Sanskrit legends; a melancholy that is both personal and literary; the child's eye of the colonial city.
intellectual_concerns: The Sanskrit epics and the Hindu legend; death and bereavement; the meeting of Indian and European culture; the position of the Indian woman; the colonial city of Calcutta; the loss of home.
historical_significance: Toru Dutt is the founding figure of Indian-English poetry: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan is the first English retelling of the Indian epics by an Indian writer, and her translations from French were praised by Edmund Gosse. She is a central figure in the history of Indian writing in English and of colonial literary culture.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jamaican-Scottish; the travel narrative and the memoir of the Crimean War
literary_identity: Nurse, traveller and memoirist; the author of Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands, one of the great Victorian autobiographies of travel and war.
biography: Born Mary Jane Grant in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805, the daughter of a Scottish army officer and a free black Jamaican woman who kept a boarding house; she learned nursing and doctoring from her mother and travelled to England, the Bahamas, Haiti and Cuba. She went to the Crimean War in 1855 after being refused by the official nursing service, ran the British Hotel behind the lines at Balaklava, and was present at the siege of Sevastopol. Her autobiography was published in 1857; she died in London on 14 May 1881.
literary_profile: Seacole wrote the memoir of a black woman's professional life in the British Empire: her narrative is comic, sharp, practical and unsentimental, and it records a journey through the colonial world — Jamaica, Panama, the Crimea — from a position that no other Victorian writer occupied. She writes as a businesswoman and a healer, claims her place at the front as a matter of right, and gives one of the very few first-hand accounts of the Crimean War by a woman of colour.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person comic narrative with direct address to the reader; anecdotes of travel and medicine; the commercial traveller's eye for trade and provisions; self-deprecating irony that carries a serious claim to recognition.
intellectual_concerns: Race and the black subject of the British Empire; nursing and the professional woman; travel and the colonial world; the Crimean War and the army; commerce and self-making; the claim to belong.
historical_significance: Seacole is the most remarkable black British woman writer of the Victorian period: her memoir is a founding text of black British autobiography, a central account of the Crimean War and a permanent record of a black woman's professional life in the empire. Her exclusion from the official nursing service, and her presence at the front as an independent businesswoman, have made her a central figure in the history of race and medicine.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English-Canadian; the emigrant memoir and the colonial sketch
literary_identity: Writer and settler; the author of Roughing It in the Bush, the classic English memoir of Canadian settlement.
biography: Born Susanna Strickland at Bungay, Suffolk, on 6 December 1803, the sister of Agnes Strickland and Catharine Parr Traill; she was an abolitionist and an early contributor to the anti-slavery album of 1826. She married the half-pay officer John Wedderburn Dunbar Moodie in 1831 and emigrated to Upper Canada in 1832, settling first in the bush near Peterborough and later at Belleville. She wrote for the Literary Garland and the Montreal newspapers, and published Roughing It in the Bush (1852), Life in the Clearings (1853) and her novel Mark Hurdlestone. She died in Toronto on 8 April 1885.
literary_profile: Moodie wrote the emigrant experience as a woman's ordeal: Roughing It in the Bush is a series of sketches of settlement in the backwoods of Upper Canada, in which the genteel Englishwoman confronts hunger, childbirth, fire, drinking neighbours and the loss of everything her class had taught her to value. It is the finest English account of the Canadian frontier and one of the most important documents of nineteenth-century emigration.
stylistic_characteristics: Episodic sketch narrative in the manner of the periodical; the first-person testimony of the gentlewoman turned settler; comic and grim anecdote; the description of the bush as an alien and hostile world; the poem embedded in the prose.
intellectual_concerns: Emigration and the settler's ordeal; the colonial woman and her household; class and gentility in the bush; the Canadian winter and the wilderness; drink and violence; religion and consolation.
historical_significance: Roughing It in the Bush is the central English memoir of Canadian settlement and one of the great Victorian accounts of emigration: it shaped the English image of Canada and is a foundational text of Canadian literature, of the literature of the frontier and of women's settler writing.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Chartist poem, the ballad and the political novel
literary_identity: Chartist leader, poet and novelist; the most gifted poet of the Chartist movement and its most effective orator.
biography: Born in Berlin on 25 January 1819, the son of a British diplomat; he was educated at London and Göttingen and came to England in 1844, where he joined the Chartist movement and edited the Northern Star and the Labourer. He was imprisoned for sedition in 1848-50, was elected to the Chartist National Assembly, and in 1852 tried to restructure the movement; he later practised as a barrister and stood unsuccessfully for parliament. He died in Manchester on 26 January 1869.
literary_profile: Jones wrote the poetry of political revolution: his Chartist songs and ballads were written for mass meetings and for the pages of the Northern Star, and 'The Song of the Lower Classes' and 'The Factory Slave' are among the most effective political poems in English. His novel The Gold Harp is a Chartist romance of the medieval peasant and the modern worker, and his poems are the most important body of working-class verse between Burns and Morris.
stylistic_characteristics: Ballad and song forms with heavy refrain; the direct address of the platform orator; the vocabulary of the Rights of Man; the industrial imagery of mill, furnace and prison; a deliberately popular diction.
intellectual_concerns: The rights of labour and the Charter; the prison and the political prisoner; the factory and the mine; the solidarity of the workers; Ireland and the United Kingdom; the history of popular resistance.
historical_significance: Jones is the central poet of Chartism and the most important English political poet between Shelley and Morris: his songs were sung at mass meetings across Britain, and his verse is the essential literary record of the first mass working-class movement in history.
